title: Forecasting 'tipping points' with AI climate simulation
source_used: Earth.com (same story; the Phys.org original could not be opened, HTTP 403)
key_facts: Researchers at Caltech, the University of Colorado Boulder and NVIDIA trained an AI system to forecast tipping points.
It uses a recurrent neural operator (RNO), an AI model with memory of how a physical system changes over time.
Trained only on pre-tipping data, it predicted a simulated climate tipping point, the disappearance of low marine stratocumulus clouds, more than two years ahead, off by about 11 days.
It was also applied to aerodynamic stall on a simulated wing and in tests it beat other AI models, especially at longer horizons.
Senior author Anandkumar of Caltech says it was demonstrated on a simplified climate model and a model of air turbulence.
The study is published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences and has been cited in a UN report on tipping points.
It could eventually help with ecosystems and disease outbreaks.
quote_evidence: In the simulated climate scenario, the AI predicted the cloud-disappearance tipping point more than two years in advance, missing the actual transition by only about 11 days.
“We demonstrated it on a simplified climate model and a model of air turbulence over a wing – systems that weren’t tractable with earlier methods.”
The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
why_it_matters_hint: Years of warning before abrupt climate shifts would help planning, but this was shown only in simulations.
event_date: Reported 16 Oct 2026 (PNAS publication date not stated)
